title: Carottes Vichy
subtitle: Glazed carrots in butter and sugar
excerpt: Carrots cut into rounds and braised slowly in butter with a little sugar and water until the liquid evaporates and the carrots are glazed and just tender. A classic French side dish that takes 20 minutes.
sourceNotes: Carottes Vichy takes its name from the spa town of Vichy in the Auvergne, famous for its mineral water. The classical recipe traditionally uses Vichy water for the braising liquid; plain water produces an identical result. Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), establishes this as a standard vegetable preparation. The technique is one of the foundational French methods for glazing root vegetables.

content.text: Carottes Vichy is the French way of glazing carrots. The carrots braise in a small amount of water with butter and sugar. The pan is covered first so the carrots cook through; then the lid comes off and the liquid reduces until the carrots are coated in a sweet, shiny glaze. It takes around 20 minutes and is considerably more interesting than plain boiled carrots.

items.prepNote: peeled and cut into 5 mm rounds or small batons

content.text: Place the carrot rounds in a single layer in the sauté pan. Add the butter, sugar, and a good pinch of salt. Pour in enough cold water to just barely cover the carrots, about 150 to 200 ml.
Bring to the boil, then cover with a lid and cook over medium heat for 10 to 12 minutes until the carrots are tender when pierced with a knife.

Remove the lid and increase the heat to medium-high. Cook, swirling the pan occasionally, for 4 to 5 minutes until the water has completely evaporated and the butter and sugar have formed a shiny glaze around the carrots. Watch carefully at this stage, the glaze can burn in seconds once the water is gone.
The finished carrots should be glossy and lightly caramelised. Season with pepper, scatter with parsley, and serve immediately.

items.symptom: The glaze has burnt and the carrots are bitter
items.cause: The water evaporated before the carrots were tender, and the heat was not reduced.
items.fix: Add a small splash of water and reduce the heat. The transition from perfect glaze to burnt caramel takes seconds, watch closely and swirl the pan once the water is nearly gone.

items.symptom: The carrots are not tender after 12 minutes with the lid on
items.cause: Too little water was added, or the carrots were cut too thick.
items.fix: Add a little more water, replace the lid, and cook for a further 3 to 4 minutes. The carrots should be completely tender before you remove the lid to glaze.

items.symptom: There is no glaze, just watery butter
items.cause: Too much water was added and the liquid never concentrated enough to form a glaze.
items.fix: Continue simmering uncovered over high heat until the liquid reduces to almost nothing, then swirl to coat. The glaze depends on the butter and sugar concentrating as the water evaporates.

content.text: The link with Vichy is culinary legend. The town's famous mineral water was said to improve the flavour when used instead of plain water. In practice, plain water gives the same result. Vichy in the Auvergne was a famous spa town in the 19th century and its name attached to several dishes of the period. The technique itself, braising root vegetables in butter, sugar, and water, is basic to French cooking and works equally well with turnips, pearl onions, and other vegetables.
